extracted.intended_audience: short-fiction authors, magazine editors, and other stakeholders in small/independent fiction magazines
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and editorial perspective on handling open submissions for a science fiction/fantasy magazine, with particular focus on responses to AI-generated submissions, maintaining inclusivity, and operational safeguards. Relevant to editors setting policy and authors submitting work.

rubrics_metrics.name: No consideration of generated texts
rubrics_metrics.description: House policy: we wouldn’t consider generated texts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision based on unanswered legal and ethical concerns over the true ownership of said works and pending court cases regarding the use of copyrighted materials in the training of generative systems. Not framed as fear of 'AI' replacing authors; rather, about ownership and legality. The editor explicitly states generated submissions were banned and some submitters were banned for trying to submit them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal and ethical concerns about ownership and training data
rubrics_metrics.description: There are currently unanswered legal and ethical concerns over the true ownership of works produced by generative systems and pending court cases about the use of copyrighted materials in training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These concerns are a primary reason for refusing generated texts. Editors should factor in ongoing litigation and unresolved rights questions when crafting policy about accepting or publishing model-generated content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain open, inclusive submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep the door open to all authors, everywhere; be 'militant' about open submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid changes that disproportionately impact new, disadvantaged, or international authors. The editor argues that short fiction is a critical feeder for the genre and that unfriendly practices would close doors for future writers and harm diversity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid gatekeeping solutions that disproportionately harm marginalized authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject proposals like charging submission fees, using paper-only submissions, accepting only known authors, soliciting only, banning countries, or requiring identity verification that would disproportionately impact new, disadvantaged, or international authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These solutions create financial or geographic barriers and are described as unacceptable for a magazine committed to inclusivity and the future health of the field. The editor calls such measures 'unfriendly submissions practices' with unacceptable consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not adopt knee-jerk exclusionary measures
rubrics_metrics.description: When faced with an onslaught of low-quality or automated submissions, resist immediate proposals that would close access (e.g., solicit-only, country bans).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead, pursue solutions that preserve access while addressing abuse. The editorial voice suggests long-term, measured countermeasures rather than reactive restrictions that harm legitimate authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality-based rejection: AI-generated works were often very poor
rubrics_metrics.description: Generated works were 'among the worst submissions we’ve ever received and sometimes bad in entirely new ways.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors can and should reject on quality grounds; the piece implies that AI-generated pieces often fail basic standards of craft, originality, and coherence in ways that make them easy to justify rejecting, separate from legal/ethical considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware 'make money with ChatGPT' schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: Many generated submissions came from people following side-hustle/blog/YouTube/TikTok schemes promising easy income via mass-generating content with ChatGPT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These schemes are often scams designed to drive paid courses; the volume of submissions generated this way was intentional (to create a 'problem' for upsell). Editors should recognize this as a scam vector rather than genuine new authorship activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for detection/countermeasures (spam-filter approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Talk of 'how can we build something like a spam filter for submissions?' — build countermeasures to manage automated or mass low-quality submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should explore spam-filter-like systems tailored to submissions, drawing lessons from tangential fields (credit-card fraud prevention, network security). Expect an arms race: technology and abusers will evolve, so countermeasures must too.

rubrics_metrics.name: Current detection tools are unreliable and possibly PR-driven
rubrics_metrics.description: Reliable detection methods do not exist and what is available has had the appearance of an afterthought, PR control, or source of potential revenue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely unquestioningly on vendor detection claims; validate tools carefully. Be skeptical of 'detection' as a finished solution and plan for ongoing adaptation and human oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational capacity and workload management
rubrics_metrics.description: The sheer speed and output of generative systems can bury editors in submissions; quantity became unsustainable (e.g., 50 generated submissions the morning of closure, over 500 in 20 days).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magazines must consider workflow, staffing, and technical systems to handle sudden volume spikes. Practical steps (even small) enabled reopening; expect possible future closures if capacity is exceeded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishers and platform responsibility for mitigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Executives and investors rushed applications out with insufficient guardrails, ignoring responsibility to provide tools to protect users and downstream targets like editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should advocate for vendor accountability and look for partners; companies should build misuse mitigations, not treat detection as PR or revenue stream.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve the role of short fiction as a risk-taking feeder for the field
rubrics_metrics.description: Short fiction publishers are more inclined to take risks and serve as feeders to novels and other media, so access must be preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy choices should account for the genre ecosystem: closing submission pathways reduces opportunities for emerging writers and harms the long-term health of the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborate and seek like-minded partners
rubrics_metrics.description: We can’t solve the problem alone; the editor hopes to find like-minded people to help build solutions to keep submissions open.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should share ideas with other magazines, submission-system developers, and experts in tangential fields to build sustainable defenses while preserving openness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent communication when policy changes occur
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor posted announcements via social media, answered press inquiries, and explained the rationale for temporarily closing submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When imposing temporary closures or policy changes, be transparent with authors and the public about reasons, enforcement, and intended next steps; public attention can also surface useful expert advice.
